title: Construct the Array
directAnswer: Count arrays of length n with values in [1, k], where a[0] = 1, a[n−1] = x, and consecutive elements differ. Track two counts: `same` = number of valid prefixes whose current element equals the target x, and `diff` = number whose current element is anything except x. The transitions are pure combinatorics: to land on x next you must come from a non-x element (diff ways), and to land on a non-x element you can come from an x-element via any of (k−1) choices or from a non-x element via (k−2) choices (excluding both x and the current value). Take everything mod 1e9+7. Answer = same after n steps. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Two-bucket counting DP (ends-at-x vs ends-elsewhere), modular
remember.formula:
MOD = 1e9+7
same, diff = (1 if x==1 else 0), (0 if x==1 else 1)   # length-1: a[0]=1
for i in 2..n:
    new_same = diff                       # only a non-x can step onto x
    new_diff = same*(k-1) + diff*(k-2)     # step onto a non-x value
    same, diff = new_same % MOD, new_diff % MOD
answer = same
rules: Bucket states by **value class**, not by value: 'equals x' vs 'not x'. All non-x values behave identically, so one count suffices for the whole bucket.
`new_same = diff`: you can only arrive at x from something that isn't x (consecutive must differ), and there's exactly one value x to land on.
`new_diff = same·(k−1) + diff·(k−2)`: from an x-element any of the other (k−1) values is non-x; from a non-x element you exclude both the current value and x → (k−2).
Reduce **every** arithmetic step mod 1e9+7, including the multiplications — products of two ~1e9 counts overflow 32-bit and even flirt with 64-bit if you batch them.
Seed the base case from a[0] = 1: if x == 1 the length-1 array already ends at x (same=1), otherwise it ends elsewhere (diff=1).
whenToUse: Count sequences/arrays under adjacency constraints (consecutive differ, no two equal, etc.)
States collapse into a few equivalence classes you can count in bulk
Answer required modulo a large prime → modular counting DP
Walks on a complete-graph-like structure with fixed start and end
antiSignals: You must enumerate or output the arrays, not count them → backtracking, not DP
Constraints couple non-adjacent positions arbitrarily → richer state needed
Values aren't interchangeable (each has distinct rules) → can't bucket into 2 classes
No modulus and n is tiny → a closed-form or direct formula may be simpler
remember.takeaway: When counting constrained sequences, group states into equivalence classes you can count together — here just 'ends at x' and 'ends elsewhere'. Two rolling counters and careful modular arithmetic turn an exponential enumeration into an O(n) recurrence.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you bucket the k possible end-values into two equivalence classes (x vs not-x) and write a correct combinatorial recurrence, applying the modulus at every step.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Tracking k separate counts (O(n·k) and unnecessary), getting the (k−1) vs (k−2) multipliers backwards, or forgetting to mod the multiplications and overflowing.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the two-class recurrence from first principles (why k−1 and why k−2), then mention the O(log n) closed form via modular inverse for huge n.

problemStatement:
Consider an array of `n` integers, where each element is between `1` and `k` (inclusive). You must build such an array subject to:

1. The **first** element is `1` (a[0] = 1).
2. The **last** element is `x` (a[n−1] = x).
3. Every pair of **consecutive** elements is **different** (a[i] ≠ a[i−1]).

Return the number of such arrays, **modulo 1e9 + 7**.
understanding: Picture building the array left to right. Each new element just has to differ from the one before it — nothing else couples positions. So at every step the only thing about the past that matters is whether the current element is the target value x or not. That two-way distinction is enough to count all continuations, and the counts multiply by how many legal next-values each class has.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the first element be something other than 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — a[0] is fixed at 1. That fixes the base case: a length-1 array is just [1], which 'ends at x' only if x = 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must every value 1..k actually appear?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Values may repeat (as long as not adjacent) and some may never appear. We're counting all arrays satisfying the three rules.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why only two states instead of k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Because all values except x are interchangeable for counting purposes — the number of ways to continue from any non-x value is identical. Collapsing them into one bucket gives O(n) instead of O(n·k).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is the modulus applied so aggressively?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Counts grow like (k−1)ⁿ, astronomically large. The product same·(k−1) can exceed 10¹⁴, so reduce after every add and multiply to stay in range and keep the answer exact mod 1e9+7.

examples.explanation: Arrays of length 4 starting at 1, ending at 2, no equal neighbours: [1,2,1,2], [1,2,3,2], [1,3,1,2]. Exactly 3.
The two-bucket recurrence yields same = 20 after 5 steps (verified by direct enumeration).
Ending back at 1: [1,2,1] and [1,3,1]. Two arrays.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse over Every Next Value
approaches.whenToMention: State it to expose the branching and the overlapping subproblems, then bucket and memoize.
hints: Build the array position by position. At each step, try every value 1..k that differs from the previous element, and recurse.
Count an array only when you reach length n with the last value equal to x.
There are up to (k−1) choices per step → (k−1)ⁿ leaves. But the count of continuations depends only on (position, previous value) — heavily overlapping.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Up to (k−1) branches at each of n positions gives O(kⁿ) leaves; recursion depth O(n).
approaches.explanation:
The literal interpretation: grow the array one slot at a time, branching on every legal next value.

**The recursion.** Define `f(i, prev)` = the number of ways to complete the array from position `i` given that position `i−1` holds value `prev`. At position `i` try every value `v ≠ prev` in `[1, k]` and sum `f(i+1, v)`. The base case at `i = n` returns 1 if `prev == x`, else 0. Start with `f(1, 1)` since `a[0] = 1` is fixed.

**Why it counts correctly.** Each root-to-leaf path is a distinct valid array (consecutive-different is enforced by `v ≠ prev`), and we tally only those ending at `x`. No array is counted twice because the choices at each position are disjoint.

**Why it's hopeless at scale.** Each position fans out to `k−1` children, so the tree has `(k−1)ⁿ` leaves — for `n = k = 10⁵` this is beyond astronomical. Yet `f(i, prev)` depends only on `i` and on *whether `prev` equals `x`* (all non-x previous values give the identical count). That means there are really only `2n` distinct subproblems hiding behind exponentially many calls — the cue to bucket and memoize.
approaches.insight: The count of continuations from a position depends on the previous value only through 'is it x or not'. Recognising that all non-x values are interchangeable collapses k branches' worth of distinct states into just two — turning O(kⁿ) into O(n).

dryRun.intro: f(i, prev): ways to finish ending at x=1. Start a[0]=1.

pitfalls: Tracking the exact previous value as state — k× more states than needed.
Forgetting the modulus, overflowing the running sum.
Running it for n, k = 10⁵ — (k−1)ⁿ never returns.

approaches.name: Two-Bucket Counting DP (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'count ends-at-x vs ends-elsewhere with combinatorial transitions'.
hints: Collapse the k end-values into two classes: `same` = arrays whose current last element is x, `diff` = arrays whose last element is anything but x.

To extend onto x: the previous element must not be x → new_same = diff. To extend onto a non-x value: from an x-element you have (k−1) non-x targets; from a non-x element you exclude both x and the current value → (k−2). So new_diff = same·(k−1) + diff·(k−2).
Base case from a[0]=1: same = (x==1), diff = (x!=1). Iterate to length n, mod everything, answer = same.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One loop of n−1 steps, each doing O(1) modular arithmetic → O(n) time. Two rolling counters → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Bucket the end-value into two equivalence classes and count each class in bulk.

**States.** After fixing the first `i` elements, let `same` be the number of valid arrays whose `i`-th element equals `x`, and `diff` the number whose `i`-th element is some value other than `x`. Every array of length `i` falls into exactly one bucket, so `same + diff` is the total count of valid length-`i` prefixes.

**Transition to length i+1.**
- *Landing on x* (`new_same`): the next element is `x`, which must differ from the current one, so the current element cannot be `x`. Only `diff` arrays qualify, and there's exactly one value (`x`) to place → `new_same = diff`.
- *Landing on a non-x value* (`new_diff`): 
  - From a `same` array (current element is `x`): any value except `x` is both legal (differs from `x`) and non-x → `k − 1` choices.
  - From a `diff` array (current element is some `y ≠ x`): the next value must differ from `y` and must not be `x`, so we exclude two values (`y` and `x`) → `k − 2` choices.
  - Total: `new_diff = same·(k−1) + diff·(k−2)`.

**Base case.** The array starts at `a[0] = 1`. So the length-1 array is `[1]`: it ends at `x` iff `x == 1`. Set `same = (x == 1 ? 1 : 0)`, `diff = (x == 1 ? 0 : 1)`.

**Modular discipline.** Counts blow up like `(k−1)ⁿ`. Apply `% MOD` after the addition *and* keep the multiplications in 64-bit (`long`) before reducing, since `same·(k−1)` with both near `10⁹` reaches `~10¹⁸` — fine for `long`, overflow for `int`. Add the two terms, then reduce.

**Answer.** After iterating up to length `n`, `same` holds the number of arrays ending at `x` — exactly what the problem asks.
approaches.insight: The k values aren't all distinct for counting — only the target x is special. Splitting into 'is x' / 'is not x' is the equivalence-class reduction that powers the whole solution; the (k−1) vs (k−2) multipliers fall straight out of 'how many legal next values does each class have'.

dryRun.intro: a[0]=1 ≠ x → same=0, diff=1. Multipliers: k−1=2, k−2=1.

code.python:
def count_array(self, n: int, k: int, x: int) -> int:
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    same = 1 if x == 1 else 0
    diff = 0 if x == 1 else 1
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):
        new_same = diff % MOD
        new_diff = (same * (k - 1) + diff * (k - 2)) % MOD
        same, diff = new_same, new_diff
    return same % MOD

java.explanation: Base case: the length-1 array [1] ends at x only when x is 1.
Only a non-x element can be followed by x.

java.line: long newDiff = (same * (k - 1) % MOD + diff * (k - 2) % MOD) % MOD;
java.explanation: (k−1) from an x-element, (k−2) from a non-x element; mod each product.
Arrays ending at x after n elements.

python.explanation: Seed the ends-at-x bucket from a[0]=1.
Step onto x only from a non-x previous element.
Python ints don't overflow, but mod keeps the value small and exact.
Final ends-at-x count is the answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop never runs; same=1 → answer 1 (the array [1]).
same=0; answer 0 — a length-1 array can only end at 1.
same toggles back: len2 same=0 diff=2... ends same=2 → [1,2,1],[1,3,1].
k−2 = −1; only n=1,x=1 is valid → 1, all longer arrays impossible (no different neighbour).

pitfalls: Swapping (k−1) and (k−2) — the x-element class has one more legal target than the non-x class.
Using int for the products — same·(k−1) overflows; use long and mod each factor.
Mis-seeding the base case (e.g. same=1 regardless of x) — a[0]=1 dictates it.

approaches.name: Closed Form via Modular Inverse — O(log n)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention for very large n: a direct formula using fast exponentiation and Fermat's inverse.
hints: The recurrence has a closed form. Walks of length n−1 on the complete graph Kₖ from a fixed start: the count splits by whether the end equals the start's value class.
Division mod a prime is multiplication by the modular inverse: divide by k using k^(MOD−2) (Fermat's little theorem).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Fast modular exponentiation for (k−1)^(n−1) and for the inverse of k each take O(log n) (or O(log MOD)) multiplications → O(log n) total.
approaches.explanation:
The two-bucket recurrence is linear, so it has a closed form — useful when `n` is enormous and even O(n) is too slow.

**The formula.** Building the array is equivalent to counting walks of length `n−1` on the complete graph `K_k` (every value adjacent to every *other* value) starting at the vertex `1`:
- Ending at a vertex different from the start (`x ≠ 1`): `((k−1)^(n−1) − (−1)^(n−1)) / k`.
- Ending back at the start (`x = 1`): `((k−1)^(n−1) + (k−1)·(−1)^(n−1)) / k`.

**Why a sign term.** The number of closed vs open walks oscillates with parity; the `(−1)^(n−1)` correction captures that the simple `(k−1)^(n−1)` over-counts or under-counts depending on whether `n−1` is even or odd.

**Dividing under a modulus.** You can't just divide by `k` in modular arithmetic — instead multiply by `k`'s modular inverse. Since `MOD = 1e9+7` is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives `k⁻¹ ≡ k^(MOD−2) (mod MOD)`. Compute `(k−1)^(n−1) mod MOD` and `k^(MOD−2) mod MOD` with fast exponentiation, combine, and normalise any negative intermediate by adding `MOD`.

**When to prefer it.** The two-bucket DP is simpler and plenty fast for `n ≤ 10⁵`. Reach for the closed form only when `n` can be astronomically large (e.g. given as an exponent) and you need sub-linear time. The trade-off is the subtlety of the parity sign and the modular-inverse machinery.
approaches.insight: A linear two-state recurrence is a 2×2 matrix power, which always admits a closed form. Here the eigenstructure of K_k yields the clean `(k−1)^(n−1)` term plus a parity correction — and the modular inverse is just how you 'divide by k' inside a prime field.

java.explanation: (k−1)^(n−1) via fast modular exponentiation — O(log n).
Represent −1 as MOD−1 so all arithmetic stays non-negative mod p.
Modular inverse of k via Fermat: k^(MOD−2) ≡ k⁻¹.
Multiply by the inverse to 'divide by k' under the modulus.

python.explanation: Built-in three-arg pow does fast modular exponentiation.
Parity correction term from the walk structure.
Fermat inverse of k for modular division.

pitfalls: Forgetting to add MOD before reducing a subtraction — produces a negative result.
Using floating-point division by k instead of the modular inverse — loses exactness.
Getting the parity sign or the x==1 vs x≠1 branch wrong — the two cases differ.

commonMistakes: Tracking k separate end-value counts instead of the two classes x vs not-x.
Swapping the (k−1) and (k−2) multipliers in the diff transition.
Skipping the modulus on multiplications and overflowing 32-bit (or even 64-bit when batched).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Tracking every value separately
commonMistakesDetailed.why: All non-x values are interchangeable for counting. Keeping k counters is O(n·k) and needless; two buckets suffice.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dp = [[0] * (k + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
# fills k columns per row — O(n*k)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong multipliers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: From an x-element there are k−1 non-x targets; from a non-x element you also exclude the current value, leaving k−2. Swapping them miscounts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow on the products
commonMistakesDetailed.why: same and (k−1) can each be near 10⁹; their product is ~10¹⁸, overflowing int and risking overflow if you add two such products before reducing.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int newDiff = same * (k - 1) + diff * (k - 2);  // int overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.good: long newDiff = (same * (k - 1) % MOD + diff * (k - 2) % MOD) % MOD;

The linear recurrence also yields an O(log n) closed form via modular inverse. Same counting mindset as Climbing Stairs and Decode Ways.
